name: Primary Bathroom
description: The private bathroom of the primary suite: two basins, a separated water closet, a shower, usually a tub, and increasingly a dressing bench and a linen store. It is the most expensive room per square foot in a traditional house, the loudest room in it at six in the morning, and the one most often placed directly over a formal room. Its design problems are not aesthetic. They are acoustic, thermal, and structural, and all three are decided in the first week.

history.replaced: dressing room with a fitted bath
history.note: The private bathroom attached to a principal bedchamber is Victorian and English in origin, and it was usually a converted dressing room. The AMERICAN primary bathroom as a designed room - two of everything, a compartmented WC, a separate shower and tub - is post-1960 and it is the room that grew fastest of any in the house: from roughly 45 sq ft in a 1955 custom house to 120-180 sq ft now, an area larger than the median 1950 bedroom. The reason it grew is worth naming, because it is not vanity: it is the doubling. Two people using one room at the same time on a working morning needs two basins, a WC behind a door, and a shower that is not the tub, and each of those is a real requirement that the single 5 by 8 could not meet. What was added on top of that requirement - the corner jetted tub of 1985-2005, now largely dead, and the ceremonial freestanding tub that replaced it - is fashion, and it should be argued about separately from the plan.

dimensions.critical_dimension: SIXTY INCHES OF CLEAR FLOOR BETWEEN OPPOSING FIXTURE FACES, and it is a two-person dimension rather than a code one. A person at a basin occupies 24 in of depth in front of the vanity face; two people passing behind each other need 42 in; one person passing behind another who is bent over a drawer needs 48. 21 (vanity) + 60 (clear) + 21 (opposite fixture or wall) = 102 in, 8 ft 6 in, and that is the minimum width of a real primary bath. THE SECOND NUMBER IS THE DOUBLE VANITY: two bowls need 30 in between centres to be usable and 36 to be comfortable, plus 15 in from each outer centre to a wall, so 30 + 15 + 15 = 60 in absolute and 36 + 18 + 18 = 72 in to work. A 60 in double vanity is two basins you cannot both stand at. Draw 72.

furniture.note: Bowls at 36 in centres minimum. 84 in is where it stops being a compromise. Below 60 in fit ONE bowl and a run of counter, which is a better room than two bad basins.

Needs 4 to 6 in clear of every wall to be cleaned behind, and 24 to 30 in on the approach side to get into. A freestanding tub in an alcove is the worst of both: it wants a bay of its own, ideally in front of a window, and it needs a floor-mounted filler whose supply comes up through the floor - which is a framing and a waterproofing decision, not a fixture one, and cannot be changed after the slab or the subfloor.

36 by 48 is the smallest adult shower; 42 by 60 takes a 15-18 in deep bench with the seat at 17-19 in, which is the single most useful thing in an ageing-in-place bathroom. A curbless entry needs the floor structure dropped 1 1/2 to 2 in over the shower area - decided at framing or not at all.

30 in clear width is the code; a real compartment is 36 by 66 in the clear with an OUT-swinging or pocket door, because a 24 in door swinging into a 36 in compartment leaves 12 in to stand in. The compartment is what makes the room usable by two people and it is the first thing cut for area.
14 in deep, as at linen-press. A 24 in deep linen cupboard in a bathroom is 10 in of stored damp.

furniture.item: a place to sit and a place to put a towel down
furniture.note: Never drawn, always wanted. A bench or a stool, and 18 in of dry counter that is not the basin surround.

daylight.orientation: East. This room is used at 6 am, in the dark, half the year, and a window on the morning side is worth more than any lighting scheme in it.
daylight.note: Two windows are usual and both are a privacy problem, which is why the room so often ends up with obscured glass and blinds permanently down - a window nobody opens the blind on is not a window. Solve it in plan: put the glazing where it looks at a wall, a hedge, a courtyard or the sky, not at a neighbour. A high transom band at 6 ft 6 in gives full daylight, complete privacy and needs no covering at all, and it is the most under-used device in this room.

must_adjoin.why: Direct and private. A primary bath reached through a corridor shared with anything else is not en-suite. WP-4.5: the via allowance is the mirror of the one added to primary-bedroom's rule at the same time. WP-2.1 found the gap from the bedroom's side and proposed the fix there; the rule is declared on BOTH rooms, so fixing one side left good-07 still failing from the other. A dressing room or a walk-in closet between the bedroom and the bath is the arrangement this corpus elsewhere calls the lock between them, and it satisfies the rule from whichever end it is read.

should_adjoin.why: Bedroom - closet - bathroom, with the closet as the lock. The closet door is the one you can shut at 6 am.

Stack the wet rooms. A primary bath over or beside a secondary bath shares the wet wall, the stack, the vent and very often the recirculation loop, and the saving is thousands of dollars decided in one sketch.
Where a laundry is on the bedroom floor it should share the wet wall with this room. It is the same stack and the same supply run.

must_not_adjoin.why: Not the room - the FLOOR PLATE. A primary bathroom directly above a dining room, a study or a formal room means a shower drain, a WC discharge and a fan running over people's heads at 6 am, plus a stack that has to land somewhere in the room below. Over a kitchen, another bath, a laundry, a closet or a passage: yes. Over a formal room: no.
Same reason, and this one bites in the era of the home office: a study under a primary bath is unusable for a video call at exactly the hours it is needed.

servicing.ventilation: Two extract points, not one - the shower and the WC compartment are separate volumes and a single fan in the ceiling ventilates neither. 50 cfm each intermittent, or a single 110 cfm unit with two inlets, ducted rigid to the outside. A steam shower needs a vapour-tight enclosure, a ceiling sloped at least 2 in per foot to shed condensate, and a maximum 7 ft ceiling inside the enclosure - a steam shower under a 10 ft ceiling does not work and rains on the user.
servicing.heat: The coldest room in the house by feel: stone or tile floor, high air change, occupied wet and undressed. Radiant floor heat is the right answer and it is a FLOOR ASSEMBLY decision - it changes the build-up by 1/2 to 1 1/2 in and it must be resolved with the adjacent bedroom floor level before framing. Retrofitting it means taking the tile up.
servicing.electrical: GFCI throughout; a receptacle at each basin; the WC compartment on the same fan circuit; and a lighting layout with at least three switched groups, because this room is used at 6 am and at 11 pm and wants different light each time.

style_variation.note: The room where the style most often loses its nerve: a Georgian-detailed house with a 160 sq ft bathroom in it has a room with no precedent, and the good answer is restraint - painted panelled wainscot, a marble-topped washstand rather than a fitted vanity, a plain tiled floor, and no ornament that the house does not use elsewhere.

Historically inserted into a dressing room, and that sequence - chamber, dressing room, bath - is the one to keep. It gives the bathroom an interior position where its lack of a window matters less and its noise reaches nobody.
The style that carries a large bathroom best, because a fully tiled room with a plaster vault and a deep window reveal is authentic to it and needs no joinery at all.
No such room. Inserting one produces a bungalow with a bathroom larger than its bedrooms.

Where the compartmented plan was invented - the 1960s ranch master bath with the WC and tub behind a door and the vanity outside it is the correct diagram and it is better than most of what replaced it.

The room most in need of an argument rather than a specification. Two things are worth defending against the current brief: the WC compartment, which is always cut and always missed, and a window that can be left uncovered.

code.requirement: Fixture clearances as at bathroom; shower 900 sq in and 30 in minimum dimension at the finished surface.
Shower and tub-shower valves must be pressure-balancing or thermostatic, limited to 120 degrees F.
code.conflict: A multi-head shower can exceed the flow the balancing valve was selected for; two valves on one shower is common and each must be independently compliant.

code.requirement: Waterproofing of shower receptors and walls; slope to drain 1/4 in per foot; curbless entries require a compliant linear or point drain and a structural drop.
code.conflict: The waterproofing plane and not the tile is the building element, and the commonest failure in a large primary bathroom is at the junction between the shower pan and a curbless threshold in a wood-framed floor. If the brief wants curbless, the framer must know at floor layout.

code.requirement: Exhaust ventilation, 50 cfm intermittent per fixture group.

sources: NKBA Bathroom Planning Guidelines, for vanity centre spacing and clear-floor dimensions
